hints: Focus on what hot ethanolic NaOH does, it causes dehydrohalogenation to form alkenes by removing HBr from adjacent carbons.
Notice the product clue, one achiral alkene plus a pair of enantiomers means one elimination route must destroy both chiral centres while the other route keeps one chiral centre.
Look at where Br sits relative to the methyl group, only adjacent positions allow one route to a tetrasubstituted double bond and the other route to a chiral alkene.
walkthrough:
**Check the starting material**

All four options have formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{13}\text{Br}$ and are cyclic, so check chirality. A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups attached.

For option A, $\text{1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane}$, both C1 (with Br) and C2 (with methyl) are chiral centres, so $2^2 = 4$ optical isomers exist. This fits the sample described.

**Recall the reaction type**

Hot ethanolic NaOH causes elimination of HBr, not substitution:
$$\text{R-CHBr-CH} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CH=C} + \text{Br}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
The Br leaves and an H is removed from a carbon next to it. Different neighbouring H positions can give different alkene isomers.

**Apply elimination to option A**

In 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane, Br is on C1. There are H atoms on C2 and on C6:

Remove H from C2: $\text{C1=C2}$ forms with the methyl on the double bond. This gives 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene. The double bond carbons are planar, both old chiral centres are lost, so this product is achiral.

Remove H from C6: $\text{C1=C6}$ forms with the methyl on C2 still single-bonded. Renumbered this is 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene. C3 still has methyl, H and two different ring segments, so it is still chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

**Count and conclude**

Total products from A = 1 achiral isomer + 2 optical isomers = only three isomers, with two being optical isomers of each other. This matches the question exactly, so A is the possible formula.

options.A: 1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane has two chiral centres at C1 and C2. Elimination toward C2 gives achiral 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene. Elimination toward C6 gives chiral 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene which exists as R and S forms. That is exactly three isomers with two as an enantiomeric pair.
options.B: 1-bromo-3-methylcyclohexane does have two chiral centres, but elimination of HBr from either side of C1 gives the same connectivity, 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene. This would give only two isomers (the pair of enantiomers), not three including an achiral one.
options.C: 1-bromo-1,3-dimethylcyclopentane has Br on a tertiary carbon. Elimination can remove H from two non-equivalent sides (C2 and C5) because of the methyl at C3, giving two different structural alkenes, both of which retain the chiral centre at C3. That would give up to four isomers (two pairs of enantiomers), not the observed three.
options.D: The substituted cyclobutane shown cannot give the required pattern. Its substitution pattern means elimination either destroys all chirality to give only achiral alkenes, or gives a different number of structural isomers. It does not produce one achiral product plus exactly one chiral pair.
